summary: Sets out IETF policy on the rights that contributors give when they submit material to the IETF, aiming to let authors keep as many rights as possible while allowing the work to be published and used. It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 and updates RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5378 sets the rights policy for material submitted to the IETF. Submitting material grants the IETF Trust specific permissions to publish and use it, while contributors keep other rights in their work.

who owns the copyright in an rfc
what happens when i submit an ietf contribution
subtitle: The permissions contributors grant for IETF work, and the rights they retain.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs permission to use contributions in its standards work and publications. Contributors may also have employers or other rights holders whose permission matters.
tldr.mechanism: Submitting a contribution counts as agreement to grant the IETF Trust a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide, sublicensable license, subject to the policy's terms.
tldr.outcome: Contributors retain rights in their underlying contributions, while the IETF Trust receives the specified permissions and owns copyright in most RFCs as collective works. RFC 5378 obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 and updates RFC 2026.

facts.label: License
facts.value: Perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide, sublicensable

today: RFC 5378 is a Best Current Practice published in November 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748, and updates RFC 2026.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5378 describes the rights that apply to contributions made as part of the IETF Standards Process. It aims to let the IETF and Internet community use those contributions while allowing authors to retain as many rights as possible. The policy addresses copyright and similar rights, not patent licenses.

The policy has no retroactive effect: it does not obtain additional rights from contributions made before the IETF Trust announced adoption of the procedures. The RFC says it is not legal advice. It obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748, and updates RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: This policy says what permissions apply when people contribute to IETF work. It does not change the rights attached to earlier contributions.

sections.title: What Counts as a Contribution
sections.content:
A Contribution includes material submitted for publication as an Internet-Draft or RFC, as well as statements made in the context of an IETF activity. This includes spoken comments at IETF sessions and written or electronic messages to IETF groups and lists. A statement clearly not intended as input to IETF work is not a Contribution under this policy.

A Contributor is the individual submitting the material. An Indirect Contributor materially contributed without personally submitting it. The IETF Trust is a trust established under Virginia law to hold and administer intellectual property rights for the benefit of the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: A contribution can be a document, an email, or a spoken statement made as input to IETF work. The policy also recognizes people who contributed without submitting the material themselves.

sections.title: Rights Granted to the IETF Trust
sections.content:
Contributors grant the IETF Trust a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, worldwide, sublicensable license to use protected contributions. The license covers copying, publishing, displaying, distributing, translating, and preparing derivative works, subject to any permitted notices that limit derivative works. It also permits limited reproduction of trademarks included in the contribution.

The Trust sublicenses the rights to IETF participants for use within the Standards Process and may grant other sublicenses under its guidance. This license does not grant patent rights. Contributors retain ownership of their underlying contributions, but the copyright in most published RFCs as collective works belongs to the IETF Trust.
sections.plainLanguage: The license lets the IETF Trust publish and work with contributions, including making translations. It does not transfer every right in the work or grant a patent license.

sections.title: Submission, Permission, and Confidentiality
sections.content:
By submitting a contribution, the submitter and each named co-contributor are deemed to have read and accepted the policy as a legally binding agreement. No separate signature or acknowledgment is required. Contributors are also deemed to have obtained necessary permissions from parties whose rights they reasonably and personally know may apply, such as an employer or sponsor.

Information subject to confidentiality or a restriction on dissemination cannot be submitted as a Contribution or considered in the IETF Standards Process. A notice in a contribution claiming confidentiality has no force under this policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Submitting material counts as accepting these rules. Material that must remain confidential cannot be submitted as IETF input.

sections.title: Notices and Rights Retained
sections.content:
Some standardized notices must be copied exactly into IETF Documents, including copies, derivative works, and translations. The IETF Trust maintains the Legend Instructions that specify which notices apply. The notices inform readers but do not themselves grant rights; the policy's license grants those rights.

Contributors or their sponsors retain ownership of their underlying contributions. The Trust is directed to confirm that Contributors may use their contributions as published in an RFC, but a document may not be represented as an RFC unless it is a full and complete copy or translation of the published RFC. The IETF has no duty to publish a contribution.
sections.plainLanguage: Standard notices explain the rules, but the license itself grants permission. Contributors keep their work and may reuse it, while only complete copies or translations may be presented as RFCs.
